In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the shift in competitive advantage from India to Britain in the cotton industry was due primarily to the higher wages in Britain.
the British textile industry was not competitive in the 1700's, but it was by 1850, because it had become more efficient and had a comparative advantage in the production of cotton goods.
the British cotton textile industry was not the first to industrialize.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the shift in competitive advantage from India to Britain was driven by the relative price of capital, and the relative price of labour was not important.
the competitive advantage of Britain was due to its factor prices, which induced a faster rate of technical progress.

the competitive advantage of Lancashire over India in cotton textiles was not the outcome of a technological race between the two countries, but rather of a race between technological progress and the relative price of labour.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the process of industrialisation was not inevitable, and the outcome was not preordained.
the shift in competitive advantage was driven by factor prices, and not by the availability of technology, which was the same in both countries.
factor prices, and especially the ratio of wages to raw material costs, are important for understanding international competitive advantage.
